messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Stress: Stress, Idealized Families: Happy families
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 22-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as a call center agent and has been married for just over a year. She presented for therapy following what she described as a gradual but unmistakable deterioration in her ability to function at work and at home. Her PCL-5 score of 61 places her firmly in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across her intake and first two sessions was one of a young woman holding herself together with enormous effort while quietly convinced that she is failing at everything.

The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Linh had stayed late after a work event, and a male supervisor offered to drive her home. When she declined to come inside his apartment, he did not accept that refusal. What followed happened in the front seat of his car, in a parking structure lit by a single flickering overhead light. She remembered the smell of his cologne, the hard plastic of the door handle she gripped and could not turn, and the taste of blood where she had bitten the inside of her cheek. She did not report the assault. He was her supervisor. She was certain no one would believe her, and she was equally certain that something in her had made this happen.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle into the past. It returned in fragments — a flash of the parking structure light, the taste of blood arriving without warning while she was eating dinner, a piece of the sound of his voice that did not connect to anything before or after it. These fragments felt more present and immediate to her than anything else in her life, sharper than her wedding photographs, more real than the face of her husband across the breakfast table. She could not have explained why, but she had come to believe that this was proof of something broken inside her.

Linh's work as a call center agent places her in a large open-plan office where supervisors and team leaders move through the floor throughout the day. From the moment she arrives, she identifies where the exits are, and she positions herself so that no one can approach her from behind. When a colleague moves suddenly into her peripheral vision, her whole body responds before she has any conscious thought — her chair scrapes back, her hands come up. She has been asked twice by a floor manager whether she is all right, and both times she deflected with a practiced smile, terrified of drawing attention from someone in authority. She avoids the manager's section of the floor entirely when she can, rerouting through the long way to the bathroom. A promotion she was offered three months ago — one that would have placed her on the same tier as the man who assaulted her — she quietly turned down without explanation.

At home, the strain has taken a different shape. When her husband's family visits and fills the apartment with the noise of an easy, affectionate family gathering, Linh finds herself unable to stay in the room. She steps outside under the pretense of needing air. What frightened her most about those moments was not the sadness exactly, but the sense of being excluded from something she no longer had access to — a version of normal life that felt sealed off from her. She had begun using sexual fantasy as a way of releasing tension she could not otherwise name or discharge, though this brought its own shame. She had asked her husband not to mention the assault, and he had honored this, but the silence between them on the subject had grown into something with its own weight.

She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to think directly about what happened, she would come apart entirely — that she was not the kind of person who could withstand that. She had come to believe she was inadequate in some fundamental way that the assault had revealed rather than caused. What finally brought her to seek help was an ambulance passing her bus stop one morning, its siren cutting through the street noise, and finding herself on her knees on the pavement without knowing how she had gotten there. She came to therapy not quite hoping to recover, but hoping, cautiously, to be told that trying was still possible.
